senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: (derivative of ἀγορά ‘marketplace,’ 57.207) a person who habitually idles in the marketplace
a court of justice for determining guilt or innocence
senses.comment: For languages which do not have technical terms for a court, it is usually possible to use some such phrase as ‘to be brought before a judge’ or ‘to have judges decide one’s case.’

senses.subdomain: Land in Contrast With the Sea
senses.def: a strip of land immediately bordering the edge of a body of water and gradually sloping down into the water
to have the faculty of hearing in contrast with being deaf
to receive information about something, normally by word of mouth
senses.comment: In Mark 6:29 ἀκούω clearly implies more than mere physiological hearing, for the content of the message is included as a significant element in the meaning of ἀκούω[c]. Compare also ἀκοή[d] (33.213).

senses.def: to believe something and to respond to it on the basis of having heard
to listen or pay attention to a person, with resulting conformity to what is advised or commanded
glosses: to pay attention to and obey

senses.def: to hear and understand a message
to give a judicial hearing in a legal matter
glosses: to hear a case in court
senses.comment: In some languages the most satisfactory way of speaking about ‘a court hearing’ is to describe the relationship between the principal participants. This may sometimes be done by translating ‘for a judge to listen to an accuser and a defender.’

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: to hear into the ear) to hear something in a secret setting
senses.comment: In some languages the equivalent of ‘what you hear in secret’ may be ‘what you hear when no one else is around’ or ‘what you hear whispered to you.’

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: to hear heavily with the ears) to be mentally slow or dull in comprehending
(a Semitic idiom, literally: to hear with hearing) to listen intently and with presumed continuity
pertaining to being of no advantage
to read something written, normally done aloud and thus involving verbalization
senses.comment: In areas where literacy is a relatively new factor in the culture, idiomatic expressions are often employed for reading, for example, ‘to let paper speak’ or ‘to mouth the marks on paper’ or ‘to see speech.’

senses.def: to make something total or complete
senses.comment: For another interpretation of ἀναπληρόω in 1 Thessalonians 2:16, see 68.27.

senses.def: to provide what has been lacking
to cause to happen, with the implication of fulfilling some purpose
to occupy a designated place
senses.comment: It is possible, however, to understand ἀναπληρόω in 1 Corinthians 14:16 as specifically referring to fulfilling a particular function. One could therefore translate this phrase in 1 Corinthians 14:16 as ‘one who takes part in the service as an ordinary person.’

senses.def: to conform to some standard as a means of demonstrating its purpose
to bring something to completion, with emphasis upon the process
senses.comment: For another interpretation of ἀναπληρόω in 1 Thessalonians 2:16, see 59.33.

senses.subdomain: Acceptable To, To Be Pleased With
senses.def: pertaining to causing people to be pleased, with the implication of being in contrast to God or at the sacrifice of some principle
senses.comment: The expression ‘men-pleasers’ may often be rendered as ‘those who are just trying to make people like them.’

senses.def: extension from a source which is above
senses.comment: In John 3:31 the reference of ἄνωθεν is obviously heaven, and in many languages it is essential to translate ‘he who comes from heaven is far above all.’|In John 3:3 ἄνωθεν may also mean ‘again’ (see 67.55). For ἄνωθεν as part of an idiom, see 41.53.

senses.subdomain: A Point of Time with Reference to Other Points of Time: Before, Long Ago, Now, At the Same Time, When, About, After
senses.def: a subsequent point of time involving repetition
senses.comment: In John 3:3 ἄνωθεν involves a play on the two distinct meanings of the word, namely, ἄνωθεν[b] 'again' and ἄνωθεν[a] 'from above' (see 84.13). For the idiom γεννάω ἄνωθεν, see 41.53.

senses.subdomain: Duration of Time without Reference to Points or Units of Time: Time, Spend Time, Always, Eternal, Old, Immediately, Young
senses.def: duration of time for a relatively long period in the past
(an idiom, literally: to be born again) to experience a complete change in one’s way of life to what it should be, with the implication of return to a former state or relation
senses.comment: It is also possible to understand ἄνωθεν in John 3:3 as meaning ‘from above’ or ‘from God’ (see 84.13), a literary parallel to the phrase ἐκ θεοῦ ἐγεννήθησαν in John 1:13. In John 3:3, however, Nicodemus understood ἄνωθεν as meaning ‘again’ (see 67.55) and γεννάω as ‘physical birth’ (see 23.52).

senses.def: to get off or to depart, as from a ship
(an idiom, literally: to go away into) to result in a state
to throw oneself off from some object (as from a ship)
(derivative of ἀριθμός[a] ‘number,’ 60.1) to employ numbers in determining a quantity
a son of Jacob and ancestor of an Israelite tribe
derivative of αὐλός flute
the taste of wormwood, a bitter-tasting herb used as a cure for intestinal worms; compare 3.21
senses.comment: As already noted in 3.21, the meaning of ἄψινθος in Revelation 8:11 is not that the waters turned into a particular plant but that the waters came to be as bitter as the plant in question.

senses.def: a son of Jacob and ancestor of an Israelite tribe
(derivative of βούλομαι[a] ‘to desire,’ 25.3) that which is desired, with the implication of accompanying planning and will

senses.subdomain: To Intend, To Purpose, To Plan
senses.def: (derivative of βούλομαι[b] and βουλεύομαι[a] ‘to purpose, to plan, to intend,’ 30.56) that which has been purposed and planned
to be full of some substance or objects
senses.comment: In Luke 11:39 there is a mixed figure of speech, and as a result γέμω may be interpreted as indicating a degree of intensity.

senses.def: (derivative of γυνή[a] ‘woman,’ 9.34) pertaining to being a woman
(derivative of δεσμεύω ‘to bind,’ 18.15) that which has been tied up or tied together
to think or reason with thoroughness and completeness
the content or result of one’s thorough reasoning
to argue about differences of opinion
to think that something may not be true or certain
senses.comment: In a number of languages ‘doubt’ is expressed by means of idioms, for example, ‘to have two thoughts’ or ‘to think only perhaps’ or ‘to believe only a little’ or ‘to question one’s heart about.’

senses.def: to give an object, usually implying value
to cause to happen, used particularly in relationship to physical events
to grant someone the opportunity or occasion to do something
to put or place an object, with the implication of some type of transfer of location or possession

senses.subdomain: Assign to a Role or Function
senses.def: to assign a person to a task as a particular benefit to others
senses.comment: It may be possible in some languages to render δίδωμι in Acts 13:20 as ‘he gave them judges,’ but more frequently it is necessary to use a phrase such as ‘he appointed judges to rule over them.’

senses.def: to pay or remunerate with money or other valuables
to deposit money with a banker, with the intent of earning interest

senses.subdomain: Agent in a Causative Role Marked by Verbs
senses.def: a marker of a causative relation, with otherwise almost empty semantic content
to cause people to undergo some experience, with the probable implication of something which is in retribution for something done
(an idiom, literally: to give right hands) to acknowledge an agreement establishing some relation, normally involving the actual practice of shaking hands
(an idiom, literally: to give glory to God) a formula used in placing someone under oath to tell the truth
glosses: promise before God to tell the truth

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: to give energy) to do one’s best in attempting to accomplish something
(an idiom, literally: to give oneself) to dedicate oneself to some activity in a completely willing manner, usually implying service on behalf of someone or something
(an idiom, literally: to give mouth) to cause someone to have something to say
glosses: to help someone to say something
to give someone something to say

senses.def: to produce fruit or seed (of plants)
(an idiom, literally: to give one’s life) to die willingly, with the implication of it being for some purpose
senses.comment: In a number of languages, however, one cannot speak of ‘giving one’s life.’ It may therefore be necessary to translate ‘to permit oneself to be killed’ or ‘to allow others to kill oneself.’

senses.def: thick wooden poles; used to support a roof
senses.comment: The contrast between ‘splinter’ and ‘beam’ in this context is a purposeful exaggeration, and can usually be reproduced, though in some instances a marginal note may be helpful.

senses.def: the oldest ethnic name for a Jew or the Jewish people
(derivative of εἰρηνοποιέω ‘to make peace,’ 40.4) a person who restores peace between people
senses.comment: Though in Matthew 5:9 the cessation of war is by no means excluded, the focus of meaning of εἰρηνοποιός is reconciliation between persons and not primarily to cause wars to cease.

senses.def: to shine forth from a source (occurring only in Matthew 13:43 in a figurative context)
a person in the genealogy of Jesus
to carry on a business involving buying and selling

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: to take advantage of someone by implying that what is offered is more valuable than it is
(a figurative extension of meaning of ἐνοικέω ‘to live in,’ not occurring in the NT) to remain in a place defined psychologically or spiritually
a repeated activity
senses.comment: In a number of languages, however, it may be necessary to restructure this second part of Hebrews 5:14 and translate as follows: ‘since they have often judged between good and evil, their abilities to do so are well-trained’ or ‘… they are well qualified to do so’ or ‘… they can easily and correctly do so.’

senses.subdomain: A Point of Time with Reference to Other Points of Time: Before, Long Ago, Now, At the Same Time, When, About, After
senses.def: a point of time following another point
to indicate one’s approval or agreement, sometimes only by nodding

senses.subdomain: Application and Removal of Liquids or Masses
senses.def: to smear or rub on substances such as salve or oil
(derivative of εὐαγγελίζω ‘to tell the good news,’ 33.215) the content of good news (in the NT a reference to the gospel about Jesus)
senses.comment: In a number of languages the expression ‘the gospel’ or ‘the good news’ must be rendered by a phrase, for example, ‘news that makes one happy’ or ‘information that causes one joy’ or ‘words that bring smiles’ or ‘a message that causes the heart to be sweet.’

senses.def: a relatively high point on a scale of extent and implying tension and opposition

senses.subdomain: Cloth, Leather, and Objects Made of Such Materials
senses.def: a band of leather or cloth worn around the waist outside of one’s clothing
senses.comment: A ζώνη was normally quite wide and could be readily folded. As such, it was often used to carry money (see Matthew 10:9).

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: to take courage) to become confident or courageous in the face of real or possible danger
(a figurative extension of meaning of θριαμβεύω ‘to lead prisoners of war in a victory procession,’ not occurring in the NT) to demonstrate one’s successful conquest of opposition
senses.comment: Since the leading of prisoners of war in a victory procession is at the present time a relatively rare cultural phenomenon, it may be impossible to employ such a literal rendering of θριαμβεύω. One may, however, wish to employ a marginal note to indicate the background meaning of θριαμβεύω in this context.

senses.def: to cause someone to completely triumph over
senses.comment: In a number of languages it is difficult to speak of triumphing without indicating the goal of such an event, but in 2 Corinthians 2:14 there is no specified object over which triumph occurs. It is possible to introduce Satan as the one over whom the believer is victorious (see 2 Corinthians 2:11). However, it is also possible to understand θριαμβεύω in 2 Corinthians 2:14 as being essentially similar in meaning to θριαμβεύω[a] (39.59) and thus to translate 2 Corinthians 2:14 as ‘for in union with Christ we are always led by God as prisoners in Christ’s victorious procession.’

senses.def: a degree which is sufficient
senses.comment: In some languages one can express the concept of sufficiency in 2 Corinthians 2:6 by introducing a negative, for example, ‘it is not necessary to punish such a person more.’ For another interpretation of ἱκανός in 2 Corinthians 2:6, see 78.14.

senses.def: a relatively high point on a scale of extent
senses.comment: It is also possible to understand ἱκανός in 2 Corinthians 2:6 as ‘sufficiency’ (see 78.50).

senses.def: (derivative of ἱκανότης ‘adequacy,’ 75.1) pertaining to being adequate for something
pertaining to a quantity which is adequate for a particular purpose
a considerable number of objects or events, probably implying what could be expected under the circumstances
a relatively large quantity, probably implying what could be expected under the circumstances

senses.subdomain: Acceptable To, To Be Pleased With
senses.def: (an idiom, literally: to do what is enough) to cause someone to be pleased by doing what will satisfy
glosses: to act in a pleasing manner

senses.def: the amount of money required to release someone who has been held in custody
glosses: the amount of money required for release
senses.comment: It may be necessary in a number of languages to be very specific about the meaning of ἱκανόν, for example, ‘the amount of money which had to be paid in order for someone to be released from arrest.’

senses.def: the wife of Chuza, an official of Herod Antipas

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: an evil disposition leading one to habitually engage in malicious acts
pertaining to being clearly evident and hence easily understood
to make someone completely adequate or sufficient for something
glosses: to cause to be fully qualified
senses.comment: In the context of Luke 6:40, however, it may be useful to translate κατηρτισμένος as ‘one who has been fully trained.’

senses.def: to cause to happen by means of some arrangement
to create, with the implication of putting into proper condition
a small island south of Crete
a secondary woody stem arising from the trunk or bough of a tree or shrub
glosses: branch (of a tree or woody shrub)
senses.comment: Some languages distinguish carefully between two major types of branches those which are essentially leaves (as in the case of palms) and those which have a number of buds or potential branches. Other languages may make a distinction between branches of a plant which is woody (a perennial) and those which are relatively soft and flexible, typical of an annual plant.

senses.def: a city or town with special privileges in that the inhabitants of such a town were regarded as Roman citizens (such towns were originally colonized by citizens of Rome)
senses.comment: A translational equivalent of ‘colony’ is frequently a phrase, for example, ‘a city where people were Romans’ or ‘a city of people who regarded Rome as their hometown.’

senses.def: to knock on a door, as a means of signaling one’s presence to those inside
senses.comment: A literal rendering of κρούω in Matthew 7:7 may be misleading in a number of languages, since in some areas only thieves knock on doors. This is done in order to determine whether anyone is at home, in which case, of course, the thief runs off. The more general practice for signaling one’s presence may be to cough, to clap the hands, or to call out one’s name.

senses.def: pertaining to being bright or shining, either of a source or of an object which is illuminated by a source
pertaining to being clear and also bright
pertaining to being brilliant or splendid, though with the possible implication of ostentatious or superficial
senses.comment: See note at 79.21.

senses.def: the act of collecting contributions, especially those involving voluntary response
senses.comment: In some instances it may be important to translate λογεία as ‘to receive gifts of money,’ but the focus is upon the activity of the person or persons engaged in obtaining the contributions. This may be expressed in some instances as ‘to go from one person to another to receive their contributions.’

senses.def: pertaining to being happy, with the implication of enjoying favorable circumstances
senses.comment: The passive construction in Matthew 5:7 (ἐλεηθήσονται) is generally regarded as a so-called ‘passive of avoidance,’ that is to say, the use of a passive form in order to avoid a direct reference to God.

senses.def: to translate from one language to another
senses.comment: In a number of languages the equivalent of ‘to translate’ or ‘to interpret’ is an idiomatic expression, for example, ‘it comes out in our language as’ or ‘in our words it means’ or ‘in our mouths it says.’

senses.def: to cause a change of state, with emphasis upon the difference in the resulting state
glosses: to cause to be different from

senses.def: a construction for the burial of the dead; often a natural cave or hewn out of bedrock
senses.comment: In a number of languages it is important to distinguish clearly between a grave (a hole in the ground in which a corpse is placed) and a tomb (a construction built above the surface of the ground for housing a corpse). In some contexts, however, it may be better to use a more generic expression, for example, ‘places where people are buried’ or ‘places where corpses are placed.’ In Mark 5:2 it is important to avoid a term which would designate merely graves, for the demoniac who met Jesus was not living down in graves in the ground, but had found some habitation either in burial caves or in tombs constructed above ground.

senses.def: a city in southern Galilee
to give or to establish a law
senses.comment: Though in English it is normal to speak of ‘giving a law,’ such an expression can be entirely misleading, since in some languages ‘to give a law’ can mean ‘to annul a law’ in the sense of giving back to people a rule or regulation. A more frequent expression for ‘giving a law’ may be ‘commanding a law’ or ‘ordering a law.’

senses.def: a room or quarters where one may stay (normally a part of a house)
senses.comment: In Acts 12:7 οἴκημα is used to refer to a prison cell, and in this context it is best translated as ‘room’ or ‘room in the prison.’

senses.def: pertaining to joint activity in some occupation or craft
glosses: having the same kind of work

senses.def: an offspring whose parents either are no longer alive or no longer function as parents (as the result of having abandoned their offspring)
senses.comment: Some languages make a distinction in terms for ‘orphan’ by indicating whether the child has been abandoned or whether one or both of the parents are dead. In languages where some indication of relative age must be introduced in speaking of ‘orphans,’ it is preferable in James 1:27 to use a term which pertains to young children.

senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of ὀρφανός[a] ‘orphan,’ 10.40) one who is without associates who may be of sustaining help
to suffer pain
senses.comment: In 1 Peter 4:13 the phrase τοῖς τοῦ Χριστοῦ παθήμασιν ‘in the sufferings of Christ’ may mean ‘the sufferings experienced at the time of the Messiah,’ that is to say, ‘the Messianic woes.’ See also 24.87.

senses.def: to experience strong physical desires, particularly of a sexual nature

senses.subdomain: Not Able To Be Known, Secret
senses.def: to cause something to be unknown or to be known only with great difficulty
glosses: to cause to not be known

senses.def: (derivative of Παρθία ‘Parthia,’ not occurring in the NT) a person who is a native of Parthia, a region southeast of Media
to experience sadness or grief as the result of depressing circumstances or the condition of persons
to place something around an object or area
to cause a state with regard to some object
a strong desire to acquire more and more material possessions or to possess more things than other people have, all irrespective of need

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: to take advantage of someone, usually as the result of a motivation of greed
senses.comment: It is also possible to understand πλεονεξία in 2 Corinthians 9:5 as referring to ‘compulsion.’

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: an evil, wicked nature
senses.comment: In a number of languages one can speak of ‘a wicked nature’ as ‘one who is bent on doing what is wicked’ or ‘one who habitually does what is wicked.’ For the total expression in Ephesians 6:12 as a title, see 12.44.

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: deeds which are wicked and evil
to bring charges previously on the basis of presumed blame and guilt
(derivative of προσαιτέω ‘to beg,’ 33.173) one who asks for charity
to touch something lightly, normally with the finger or hand
senses.comment: For another interpretation of προσψαύω in Luke 11:46, see 18.11. Note that προσψαύω[a] differs in meaning from προσψαύω[b] ‘to touch’ (18.11) in that it is understood in a hyperbolic sense of ‘to merely touch,’ while προσψαύω[b] implies ‘doing something to help’ or ‘doing something about it.’

senses.def: to touch something, with the intent of doing something about it
senses.comment: In employing a term for ‘touch’ in Luke 11:46, it is important to use an expression which will imply ‘touching in order to relieve the burden.’ This may be done in some instances by translating ‘to help by touching’ or ‘to touch with a finger in order to help a little.’ For another interpretation of προσψαύω in Luke 11:46, see 24.75.

senses.def: to be sick with a fever
senses.comment: Though in a number of languages one can say ‘a person has a fever,’ in some languages the reverse expression is used, for example, ‘the fever has a person.’ Similarly, instead of saying ‘a person has a disease,’ it is ‘the disease which grabs a person.’ One may often speak of a fever as ‘to become hot’ or ‘to burn’ or ‘to be sick with burning.’

senses.def: dirt as refuse in contrast with soil

senses.domain: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products
senses.def: (figurative extension of meaning of σκῆνος ‘tent,’ not occurring in the NT) temporary habitation in the human body
senses.comment: Only rarely can one preserve in translation the figurative meanings suggested by the terms σκῆνος and σκήνωμα. What is significant in such contexts is the temporary nature of the dwelling, and therefore the relatively brief time which the body is to serve the person who dwells in it. In some cases it may be relevant, therefore, to have a footnote to point out the temporal aspects of this figurative usage of σκῆνος and σκήνωμα[c].

senses.def: (derivative of σπείρω ‘to sow,’ 43.6) grain growing in a field
senses.comment: In a number of languages there are distinct terms for various stages of growth of grain, and in view of the context of the account in Mark 2:23 and parallel passages, it is important to indicate that the grain was essentially ripe.

senses.def: to provide confirming evidence by means of a testimony
senses.comment: It may be necessary in some languages to translate this phrase in Romans 2:15 as ‘their consciences say to them that this is true.’

senses.def: to cause to live again together with others
glosses: to raise to life together with
senses.comment: There are serious semantic difficulties involved in a literal translation of συνεγείρω or συζωοποιέω, for a literal rendering could either be interpreted as ‘to be raised to life at the same time with’ or ‘to be raised to life in the same way as,’ but the reference in Colossians 3:1 and Ephesians 2:5 is to a spiritual existence more than to a literal resurrection of the body. This means that both συνεγείρω and συζωοποιέω must be understood as highly figurative. Hence, in Colossians 3:1 it may be necessary to translate εἰ οὖν συνηγέρθητε τῷ Χριστῷ as ‘since you have been raised to life, so to speak, with Christ’ or ‘since, as it were, you have been raised to life with Christ.’ In this way one may point to the fact of a figurative element involved.

senses.def: (derivative of συνίστημι[a] ‘to recommend,’ 33.344) pertaining to being commended or recommended
senses.comment: It may be necessary to restructure considerably the components in an expression such as ‘we need letters of recommendation to you,’ for example, ‘we need letters written to you which recommend us’ or ‘… which say, These men are good.’

senses.def: (derivative of Ταρσός ‘Tarsus,’ 93.596) a person who lives in or is a native of Tarsus
to pluck or pick by pulling off or out of

senses.subdomain: Indefinite Units of Time: Age, Lifetime, Interval, Period
senses.def: pertaining to being of an age beyond the prime of life (in 1 Corinthians 7:36 a reference to a woman beyond the normal marriageable age)
to move back to a point from which one has previously departed
(a figurative extension of meaning of ὑποστρέφω[a] ‘to return,’ 15.88) to turn back to a previous belief
glosses: to change to a former belief

senses.def: to be again in a former state

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: to experience a feeling of ill will due to real or presumed advantage experienced by someone else
deep constructions, often walled with stone, at the bottom of which was a pool of water
senses.comment: If there was a relatively ready flow of water, a well could very appropriately be called a πηγή[a] ‘spring,’ 1.78 (and this may be the reason for πηγή in John 4:6), but if water only gradually seeped into the well from surrounding areas or was collected in the well from surface drainage, it would be more appropriately called φρέαρ[a]. However, both terms are used interchangeably in certain contexts; compare, for example, πηγή in John 4:6 and φρέαρ in John 4:11, both referring to Jacob’s well at Sychar.

senses.def: a relatively deep pit or shaft in the ground
senses.comment: In this occurrence of φρέαρ (Revelation 9:1), the reference is essentially equivalent to that of ἄβυσσος ‘abyss’ (1.20).

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: to show kindness to someone, with the implication of graciousness on the part of the one showing such kindness
senses.comment: It is important to note that kindness in English indicates an activity in which an individual is kind to someone; it is essentially an event involving a particular quality. The same is true of χάρις in Acts 15:40, for this is not a mere gracious disposition, but an expectation of the Lord’s showing kindness.

senses.def: (derivative of χαρίζομαι[a] ‘to give graciously and generously,’ 57.102) that which is given freely and generously
senses.comment: χάρις[b] may also occur in contexts in which the meaning of ‘generous gift’ may imply the purpose of gaining some favor or benefit. In Acts 24:27 (θέλων τε χάριτα καταθέσθαι τοῖς Ἰουδαίοις ὁ Φῆλιξ ‘Felix wanted to be offered a generous gift by the Jews’) the implication is that of ‘a bribe,’ but probably spoken of euphemistically here as ‘a gift.’

senses.def: an expression of thankfulness

senses.subdomain: Acceptable To, To Be Pleased With
senses.def: a favorable attitude toward someone or something
senses.comment: In the expressions ἔχοντες χάριν πρὸς ὅλον τὸν λαόν (Acts 2:47) and εὗρες γὰρ χάριν παρὰ τῷ θεῷ (Luke 1:30) it would appear on the basis of superficial examination that the subject of the participle or the verb is in some respects an active agent. Semantically, however, the subject is actually the recipient of the good will, and in these contexts it is either the people or God who takes pleasure in or is pleased by the grammatical subjects in question. These expressions are typical of situations in which the semantic relationships are almost completely the reverse of the syntactic relationships.

senses.def: gold (the most highly valued metal in the ancient world)
senses.comment: Terms for gold are widespread throughout the world even as the presence of gold or knowledge about gold is likewise almost universal. Therefore, there is usually no difficulty involved in obtaining a satisfactory term for ‘gold.’

senses.def: object or objects made of gold
senses.comment: Gold jewelry may be referred to as ‘pretty things made out of gold,’ but rather than say that the woman was ‘covered with gold ornaments’ (Revelation 17:4), it may be far more appropriate to say ‘she wore many gold ornaments’ or ‘many gold ornaments were fastened to her clothes.’

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: silver and gold) a generic expression for currency
a somewhat more emphatic marker of similarity between events and states
